stories.label: The 'Lost' Villages of Myanmar's Rakhine
stories.summary: Bellingcat geolocates and verifies villages erased in western Myanmar — a survivor describes a 'river of blood', and 20 relatives including three children killed in a 2024 attack on Htan Shauk Khan. Lead with the named village and the satellite-before/after method: this is OSINT making the disappearance of Rohingya-area settlements legally legible when no court will name it. Mechanism to highlight: physical erasure of villages is the form ethnic cleansing takes once the cameras leave, and Bellingcat's frames are the documentary record that survives. The reader cares because the victims are Muslims the world stopped counting.

stories.label: US strike on alleged drug boat in Pacific kills one
stories.summary: A US military strike on a vessel it labelled a 'narco-terrorist' boat in the Eastern Pacific killed one man and left two stranded at sea — the latest in a pattern rights groups are tracking. Lead with the legal void: there was no arrest, no court, no due process, just a lethal strike on a suspected smuggler, and the Pentagon's own language ('narco-terrorist') is the tell that a law-enforcement problem has been redefined as a war target. Mechanism to teach: the post-9/11 'targeted killing' doctrine built for jihadists is migrating to drug interdiction in international waters, normalising extrajudicial execution of civilians. Al Jazeera carries it because Western wires treat the body count as routine.

stories.label: Hungary Reverses Decision to Exit International Criminal Court
stories.summary: Hungary's parliament repealed the ICC-withdrawal Orbán launched in 2025 as a gesture to Netanyahu — and the reversal comes under new PM Péter Magyar. Lead with what changed and what it signals: a single election unwound a member state's exit from the world's only permanent war-crimes court, and Israeli press is reading it as the loss of a friendly carve-out for an indicted PM. Mechanism to teach: the ICC's authority is only as durable as the domestic politics of its members, and the same machinery that nearly let Hungary shield Netanyahu can be switched off by the next government. Multi-sourced across HU, US, IL, SG and ZA — note the symmetry of how each capital frames a court that indicts the powerful.

stories.label: Big setback for opposition as Supreme Court upholds Election Commission's power to conduct S.I.R exercise
stories.summary: India's Supreme Court ruled the Election Commission acted within its powers in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, dismissing opposition petitions that the Bihar exercise risked disenfranchising voters by tying the rolls to citizenship checks. Lead with the precedent, not the politics: a court with the power to halt a roll purge instead blessed it, and that ruling now governs how every future revision can be run ahead of national elections. Mechanism to teach: who controls the voter list controls the electorate, and the SIR converts an administrative cleanup into a citizenship gate the judiciary has now declared constitutional. The reader should see this as a structural shift in Indian electoral plumbing, carried across three Indian outlets with low divergence.

stories.label: Typical energy bill set to soar by £221 a year from July as new price cap announced
stories.summary: Ofgem's new price cap lifts the typical UK household bill by £221 a year from July — the first time the Iran war's wholesale-gas spike lands directly on domestic bills. Lead with the transmission chain: a war 4,000km away over the Strait of Hormuz now shows up as a line item on a British variable tariff, and the Guardian's analyst says high prices are structural, not a spike. Mechanism to teach: the UK's exposure to global gas means its consumers are unhedged buyers of Middle East risk, and 'energy security' rhetoric has not insulated a single household. The reader sees how a geopolitical shock is metered out to ordinary people through a regulator's quarterly arithmetic.

stories.label: Byju's founder Byju Raveendran gets six-month jail term in Singapore
stories.summary: A Singapore court jailed Byju Raveendran for six months for contempt — defying asset-related court orders dating to 2024 — closing a chapter on what was once India's most-valuable startup, backed by the Qatar Investment Authority among others. Lead with the fall: a founder once worth billions on paper is going to jail not for the collapse itself but for stonewalling the courts unwinding it. Mechanism to teach: when a venture-capital darling implodes, the accountability that bites is cross-border insolvency enforcement, and Singapore's contempt power reached a founder Indian proceedings could not. The reader sees the edtech bubble's reckoning arrive through a jurisdiction chosen for its rigour, not its sympathy.

stories.label: Hong Kong beats Switzerland as world's largest offshore wealth hub, BCG finds
stories.summary: BCG data shows Hong Kong has overtaken Switzerland as the world's largest cross-border wealth hub, with offshore money booked there up 10.7% in 2025 to US$2.9 trillion on mainland inflows and an IPO bonanza. Lead with the handover of a centuries-old title: the global capital of hidden money is no longer the Alps but a Chinese SAR. Mechanism to teach: offshore wealth follows political gravity — capital is choosing a jurisdiction inside China's perimeter over neutral Switzerland, a vote about where the rich think safety and growth now sit. The reader sees the financial centre of the next era being named in a consulting firm's league table.

stories.label: Synthetic controls reveal hurricane effects on urban bee biodiversity from iNaturalist data - Nature Ecology & Evolution
stories.summary: Researchers paired citizen-science iNaturalist observations with synthetic-control methods — an econometrics tool — to show Hurricane Ida cut bee observations in Philadelphia by 15.5–20.9%. Lead with the method, because that is the news: causal inference borrowed from economics now lets ecologists measure a single disaster's hit to urban biodiversity from messy public data. Mechanism to teach: synthetic controls build a 'counterfactual city' from comparison sites, isolating the storm's effect from background noise — the same technique that evaluates policy, applied to pollinators. The reader gets why this matters: it turns the flood of amateur nature photos into rigorous evidence of how climate shocks erode the species cities depend on.

stories.label: U.S. companies have an AI problem. Indian IT wants to be the solution
stories.summary: As US firms find AI returns elusive, India's IT giants are pitching themselves as the integrators who can close the 'deployment gap' — even as the same automation threatens to eat their own back-office business. Lead with the bind: the labour pool that built the West's software is now selling the shovels for an AI gold rush that may bury it. Mechanism to teach: most enterprise AI value is stuck at the last mile of integration, and that messy middle is exactly the outsourcing work India dominates — a reprieve, but one with an expiry date as agents improve. The reader, a technically literate professional, recognises both the ROI mirage and the global-South labour story underneath it.

stories.label: US law enforcement warns of "anti-tech extremism" as AI hatred grows
stories.summary: After attacks on CEOs and a protest movement targeting data centers, US federal intelligence and domestic law enforcement are circulating reports naming a new domestic target: 'anti-technology extremists.' Lead with the move itself — the state is constructing a threat category around opposition to AI and data centers, more than 1,000 documents deep. Mechanism to teach: labelling diffuse public anger as 'extremism' is how surveillance and counterterrorism powers get extended to a political grievance, folding legitimate protest over jobs and land into the security apparatus. The reader should see the civil-liberties stakes: the backlash against AI is being criminalised before it is understood.

stories.label: Tuvalu aims to become a 'Digital Nation' amid rising sea levels
stories.summary: Tuvalu is digitising its statehood — government, records, identity and culture — to preserve sovereignty as rising seas threaten to make the islands uninhabitable. Lead with the unprecedented question it forces: can a nation exist as data when its land disappears? Mechanism to teach: statehood in international law rests on territory and population, so Tuvalu is engineering a legal-technical workaround — a 'Digital Nation' that keeps its maritime boundaries, governance and identity alive in the cloud even if the physical state drowns. The reader sees the first real test of post-territorial sovereignty, a Global-South innovation born of an emergency the world's emitters created.

stories.label: Imaging quantum chemistry in action with quantum attomicroscopy - Communications Chemistry
stories.summary: [Auto-backfill for science floor] Understanding how quantum electron and nuclei motions drive biomolecular reactions is a foundational challenge in quantum chemistry and biology. While ultrafast charge migration in DNA is theorized to influence genome stability and signaling, real-time observation remains elusive. Here, we report a

stories.label: SK Hynix Joins $1 Trillion Club on AI Memory Chip Dominance
stories.summary: SK Hynix crossed $1T market cap on HBM dominance and is filing for US ADRs — Korea now hosts the second pure AI-memory monopoly after TSMC. Lead with the structural point: the AI build-out has produced two single-country chokepoints (TSMC logic in Taiwan, SK Hynix HBM in Korea) whose valuations now dwarf entire national markets — pairs with [[taiwan-stock-market-surpasses-india-tsmc-ai-concentration]] as the same concentration story from the demand side. Mechanism: HBM yields favor incumbents because each generation requires deeper integration with NVIDIA's roadmap; Micron and Samsung can't close the gap fast enough to break the duopoly. Reader takeaway: 'AI sovereignty' debates are downstream of two Asian memory and logic fabs.

stories.label: The lender that governs
stories.summary: IMF approved Pakistan's third EFF review and added 11 new conditions — total structural conditionality now 75, with 30 standing commitments for 105 compliance requirements covering fiscal, governance, energy and trade policy. Lead with the number 105: this is no longer a 'loan with conditions', it is a parallel administration that has substituted for elected economic policy-making. Mechanism worth teaching: each review ratchets conditionality upward because compliance gaps from prior reviews are converted into new structural benchmarks — the program grows even when targets are met. Reader takeaway: Pakistan's sovereign budget process now runs through Washington, and Dawn says it plainly. Pakistan OIC; regional voice carried.

stories.label: More Than Trade: Modi's Visit to Sweden and Norway
stories.summary: Modi's Nordic tour is the opening move in India's Arctic strategy — but Russia's existing Arctic dominance is the obstacle Delhi has to negotiate around without breaking its Moscow rapport. Lead with the contradiction: India wants Arctic credentials (rare earths, shipping lanes, scientific stations) but the only northern path runs through Russian-controlled passages. Mechanism worth teaching: the Arctic is becoming the next critical-minerals theatre after Central Asia, and middle powers like India have to choose between US-aligned northern routes and Russian-aligned ones. Pairs with [[india-us-critical-minerals-rare-earths-framework-jaishankar-rubio]] as the parallel polar leg of the same minerals strategy.

stories.label: SPECIAL REPORT: Day Akwa Ibom market burned because a fire truck had no fuel
stories.summary: Premium Times investigation: an Akwa Ibom market burned to the ground because the local fire station had received 'no diesel for over two months' — traders lost stock worth millions of naira while a fueled truck sat idle. Lead with the named station and the two-month gap: this is the accountability failure rendered as a single missing fuel allocation, and Premium Times got the on-the-record admission. Mechanism worth teaching: Nigeria's fiscal devolution after subsidy removal left state-level emergency services unfunded, and the failures are now individually documented — palm oil flowing through burnt walkways while bureaucratic responsibility is dispersed across federal, state and municipal lines no one is willing to claim. Reader takeaway: 'state capacity' is not abstract; it is whether the truck has fuel on the day the market burns. Nigeria OIC; regional voice carried.

stories.label: Bangladesh measles cases: Hundreds of children die within months
stories.summary: Hundreds of Bangladeshi children dead from measles within months — a disease eliminable with a $1 dose. BBC opens on a named 4-year-old, Akira, learning English before she died. Lead with the named child and the count: this is the most preventable mass child death of the season, and it is happening in a country whose vaccination programme was a global model a decade ago. Mechanism worth teaching: measles is a herd-immunity disease, and Bangladesh's coverage dipped below the 95% threshold after pandemic-era catch-up campaigns lapsed and UNICEF funding tightened — the deaths are a delayed externality of a budgeting decision. Reader takeaway: when global vaccine financing slips, the body count appears in the Muslim-majority countries that had been the success cases. Bangladesh OIC.

stories.label: Traveller from Uganda isolated in Bengaluru after showing suspected Ebola symptoms
stories.summary: A woman who flew from Uganda via Ahmedabad to Bengaluru on 23 May was moved to Karnataka's State Epidemic Diseases Hospital after surveillance flagged fatigue and mild symptoms; samples sent to the National Institute of Virology. Lead with the routing — Uganda → Ahmedabad → Bengaluru — and the surveillance trigger: India's Ebola tracking on inbound passengers from affected regions actually caught a suspected case at the airport stage. Mechanism worth teaching: post-2014 international airport surveillance is the single most successful public-health upgrade of the last decade, and most of the catches never make headlines because samples come back negative. Reader takeaway: the system worked here — a suspected case isolated within four days of arrival — and that is the unsexy public-health infrastructure that prevents a second 2014. Flag for follow-up once NIV result is in.

stories.label: Bread&Net 2025: Explore the Outcomes Reports
stories.summary: SMEX publishes the outcome reports from Bread&Net 2025, the MENA region's main digital-rights convening — sessions on infrastructure control, platform takedowns of Arabic and Palestinian content, and surveillance baselines across Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan and the Gulf. Lead with the question the reports keep asking: who controls the digital infrastructure that Arab civil society depends on, and what does the cost of that dependence look like in 2025-2026's documented case data. Mechanism worth teaching: digital-rights work in the MENA region is increasingly a documentation exercise — these outcome reports are the institutional memory that survives even when individual orgs are shut down. Pairs with [[smex-ceasefire-digital-rights-mideast-surveillance-baseline]]. Lebanon OIC; SMEX is the regional voice.

stories.label: Cost To Link LUCAS Kamikaze Drones To Starlink Highlights Pentagon's Ever-Growing Dependence On SpaceX
stories.summary: Pentagon pushes back on reported upcharges to connect LUCAS one-way attack drones to Starlink — but the underlying story is that SpaceX's products have become 'largely essential' to US military operations, with no second supplier at parity. Lead with the lock-in: a single private satellite operator now sets the per-drone connectivity bill for a US weapon system, and the only public negotiation is over the size of the markup. Mechanism worth teaching: defence procurement was supposed to avoid monopoly suppliers by design (DoD Section 803), but LEO broadband is a winner-take-most market and Starlink's lead has converted into a procurement chokepoint the Pentagon admits is irreplaceable. Reader takeaway: 'critical infrastructure' is a category that now includes a private constellation whose owner the US government cannot replace and cannot fully discipline.

stories.label: Former President Biden sues DOJ over release of interview audio
stories.summary:
[Auto-backfill for politics floor] Former President Joe Biden sued the Justice Department on Tuesday, urging a federal judge to block the release of audio recordings and transcripts of his private conversations with the ghostwriter of his 2017 memoir.

The suit stems from a 2024 Freedom of Information Act request by the conservative

stories.summary:

* Pakistani circles 'fed up' by failure of bilateral efforts, pin their hopes on Chinese shepherding the process

CHINA'S diplomatic mediation between Pak­istan and Taliban-ruled Afghanistan is keeping hopes a

stories.label: Iran says new US strikes violate ceasefire
stories.summary: Hours after the Doha track resumed, US CENTCOM ran what it called 'defensive' strikes in southern Iran; Tehran says the truce is already broken and BBC/News18/CNA/Punch carry the same framing with sentimentDivergence 0.24. Lead with the timing collision: Rubio says a deal is 'a few days' away while the kinetic side is still firing, which is precisely the failure mode SMEX and Drop Site have been documenting — a 'ceasefire' that only stops the parts both sides agree to count. Mechanism: 'defensive strikes' is the doctrinal loophole that lets Washington keep shooting and still call it peace, and the political cost is paid by Lebanese and Iranian civilians outside the deal's perimeter. Iran arc continuation from [[iran-mq9-drone-downed-persian-gulf-irgc-ceasefire]] and [[khamenei-no-going-back-us-bases-middle-east-realignment]] — third Iran-arc slot, do not stack further this cycle.

stories.label: US and Armenia sign partnership agreement ahead of Armenian election
stories.summary: Rubio and Mirzoyan signed a strategic-partnership agreement weeks before Armenia votes — multi-sourced from AM, US, SG, IN and TR (Anadolu). Lead with the timing: Washington is putting its name on Pashinyan's re-election platform after Yerevan's pivot away from the CSTO, and Turkey's state wire is reporting it without alarm — which is itself the story, given Ankara and Yerevan's century of frozen diplomacy. Mechanism: 'strategic partnership' is the same template Washington just used with India on rare earths; the Caucasus version trades a sanctions-circumvention chokepoint between Iran and Russia for US security backing. Reader takeaway: the post-Karabakh realignment is being locked in with a US signature, and Iran is reading every line of it.

stories.label: Czech 'ammo coalition' for Ukraine loses support
stories.summary: President Petr Pavel says half the participants — 18 down to 9 countries — have walked away from Prague's Ukraine-ammunition initiative since Babis took office in December 2025, and even RT carries the story straight. Lead with the number: a coalition that was the EU's flagship workaround when Hungary blocked direct aid has been gutted in six months by a single change of government. Mechanism worth teaching: 'coalitions of the willing' depend on whichever election cycle is most recent, and that's a structural weakness Brussels has no answer to. Reader takeaway: the same week US planners briefed NATO they would cut crisis commitments to Europe, Europe's own ad-hoc Ukraine logistics is collapsing — and Moscow is the audience that benefits from both stories landing on the same day.

stories.label: Banned Russian Submunitions Found After Mali's Military Announces Airstrikes
stories.summary: Bellingcat + Jeune Afrique OSINT investigation: unexploded Russian-made cluster bomblets and impact damage documented in a northern Mali village, despite Mali being a state party to the Convention on Cluster Munitions. Lead with the treaty violation by name and the named village: this is the second documented use of banned submunitions by the Bamako–Africa Corps partnership, and the first where the geolocated craters appear in Bellingcat's frames. Mechanism worth teaching: Russia exports the weapons class Western states agreed to stop using, and a Sahelian junta is choosing them precisely because the political cost is paid by villagers no UN body will name. Mali is OIC; feed offered no Malian or regional Sahel outlet — note feed-side gap. Accountability arc, separate from Sudan-RSF-UAE [[sudan-rsf-uae-colombian-mercenaries-hrw-report]] but same supply-chain-of-violence template.

stories.label: Peace deal hopes boost Wall Street stocks despite latest US strikes
stories.summary: S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at fresh records the same day US CENTCOM hit Iran and Brent jumped on Hormuz fears — the market is pricing the strikes as a near-term deal catalyst, not an escalation. Lead with the disconnect: equity desks are betting that the next round of strikes shortens the ceasefire negotiation, while oil desks are betting it lengthens it, and both bets are running simultaneously in the same Bloomberg terminal. Mechanism worth teaching: 'risk-on' is now an Iran-war trade, with the Strait of Hormuz functioning as a put option on the broader index — the implied volatility is paid by Global South economies that don't get to hedge. Reader takeaway: the markets that determine US pension performance are now openly priced against the ceasefire holding for the shortest commercially convenient interval.

stories.label: Fatalities Reported in Washington State Packaging Facility Explosion
stories.summary: Nippon Dynawave Packaging's Longview, Washington pulp-and-packaging mill exploded Tuesday morning with fatalities and multiple critical injuries — the second mass-casualty US industrial accident in a working-age industry in six months. Lead with what the facility actually is: pulp mill chemistry runs on hydrogen sulfide, chlorine dioxide and recovery boilers operating just below their explosive limit, and the regulatory deference to operators on the West Coast packaging side is documented. Mechanism worth teaching: 'packaging' sounds benign but the upstream pulping is one of the most dangerous chemical environments outside refining, and federal inspection backlogs at OSHA are running at multi-year highs. Reader takeaway: the workplace-safety regression isn't only a Sahel-mercenary or Kazakh-oil story — it lands the same day in Longview.

stories.label: Govt plans Wapda security force for water projects
stories.summary: Pakistan is creating a dedicated paramilitary 'Wapda Security Force' to protect dams, hydropower plants, and Chinese workers at Dasu and other CPEC-linked sites, following repeated attacks on Chinese engineers. Lead with the institutional choice: water infrastructure has been promoted out of civilian policing and into a standing armed force, with the bill already sent to parliament. Mechanism worth teaching: when a state can no longer guarantee Chinese contractor safety through ordinary means, the contract terms shift — Beijing is increasingly underwriting Pakistani fiscal stress in exchange for sovereign militarisation of CPEC perimeters. Reader takeaway: the cost of CPEC is no longer just the loan book; it is the bureaucratic architecture of a parallel armed force whose mandate is set in Beijing's risk department. Pakistan is OIC; Dawn provides the regional voice.

stories.label: Want an oxygen-rich atmosphere? Stuff oxygen's friends in the mantle.
stories.summary: A new model argues Earth's oxygen-rich atmosphere required not just photosynthesis but a tectonically active mantle willing to swallow reductant minerals — taking oxygen-hungry rocks out of circulation long enough for free O2 to accumulate. Lead with the inversion of the standard schoolbook story: photosynthesis alone isn't enough; the answer is that subduction has to hide the iron and sulfide chemistry that would otherwise eat the oxygen. Mechanism worth teaching: planetary habitability is a geophysics problem as much as a biology one, and the implications for exoplanet detection are direct — a stagnant-lid world like Venus can host life chemistry but cannot store its atmospheric exhaust. Reader takeaway: the question 'why does Earth have breathable air' has a new answer this week, and it's a tectonic answer.

stories.label: Discovery of furtivovirus advances understanding of giant virus evolution
stories.summary: A newly described giant virus — 'furtivovirus' — sits awkwardly on the edge of the classical tree of life, with a genome large enough to look cellular but no cellular machinery of its own. Lead with what the name acknowledges: it hides in plain sight, between virus and proto-cell, and challenges the cleanest line biology has drawn. Mechanism worth teaching: giant viruses keep getting weirder — they encode their own metabolic enzymes, in some cases translation factors — and each new isolate forces the question of whether 'life' has one origin or several. Reader takeaway: the next major revision of the tree of life is unlikely to be a tweak; it will be a redrawn topology, and furtivovirus is one of the branches forcing the change.

stories.label: Millions of AI agents imperiled by critical vulnerability in open source package
stories.summary: A critical vulnerability in Starlette/FastAPI's ASGI handling — used as the HTTP backbone for millions of AI agents and MCP servers — lets attackers walk in and steal credentials, tool tokens, and downstream third-party access. Lead with the dependency surface: the same week the [[agentic-divide-ai-agent-inequality-global-south-productivity]] story landed, the agent stack the global North relies on turns out to be one Python web framework deep. Mechanism worth teaching: agent supply chains are concentrated on a handful of HTTP servers, and a single misparsed header propagates to every downstream tool the agent can call — the blast radius is whatever the agent's OAuth scopes added up to. Reader takeaway: 'AI agents' are not yet a security category in their own right — they inherit the bugs of 2018-era Python web servers, and the credential exposure is qualitatively worse because the agents hold delegated keys.

stories.label: Charger placement optimization in wireless sensor networks using hybrid graph coloring and Enhanced Aquila Optimization
stories.summary: A two-stage optimization framework — hybrid graph coloring + an Enhanced Aquila metaheuristic — determines both the number and location of wireless chargers in sensor networks, the layer that decides how long an IoT deployment can actually survive on harvested energy. Lead with the deployment problem: as wireless sensor networks scale from a few hundred nodes to tens of thousands (smart-grid, water-quality, AMR monitoring), charger placement is the bottleneck most operators have been solving with rules of thumb. Mechanism worth teaching: graph coloring gives the lower bound on chargers needed; the bio-inspired Aquila search then tunes positions, an order of magnitude cheaper to compute than the integer-programming formulation. Reader takeaway: this is the unglamorous algorithmic infrastructure that decides whether the world's environmental-monitoring networks can run for a decade without rip-and-replace — and the answer is now substantially better.

stories.label: US plans to slash NATO contributions - Spiegel
stories.summary: Hegseth quietly told NATO officials in Brussels the US will shrink the bombers, fighters and warships it would commit to allies in a crisis — a Spiegel scoop carried by US, Russian (RT) and Turkish (TRT World) outlets. Lead with the mechanism: this is not a public NATO communique but a private downgrade of US commitments, briefed first to a German magazine, and Moscow is the audience that benefits most from learning of it. Reader takeaway: the transatlantic security architecture is being unbundled bureaucratically rather than rhetorically — the war-time order of battle is shrinking before the political alliance does.

stories.label: Ukraine: EU summons Russian envoy after call to leave Kyiv
stories.summary: The EU, Germany and UN Secretary-General Guterres formally rebuked Moscow for telling foreign diplomats to leave Kyiv — multi-sourced across DE, US, QA (Al Jazeera) and TR. Lead with the diplomatic register: a Vienna-Convention-style evacuation warning is being treated by Europe as a threat against civilian diplomatic personnel, not a courtesy. Mechanism: this is the European response stage of the Lavrov-Rubio call already on the record — Brussels is choosing public summons over backchannel, while Washington stays quiet. Reader takeaway: the Ukraine escalation track is being kept alive by European diplomats while US bandwidth is absorbed by the Iran file.

stories.label: Atrocities in Sudan backed by Colombian mercenaries trained at UAE bases, says report
stories.summary: An HRW-anchored MEE investigation: Colombian mercenaries who carried out atrocities for the RSF in Sudan were trained at UAE bases inside the country. Lead with the supply chain of violence — named state (UAE), named recruiter pipeline (Colombian veterans), named victims (Sudanese civilians under RSF rule). Mechanism worth teaching: the Sudan war is no longer a 'civil' war in any meaningful sense — it is an outsourced campaign in which a Gulf state provides the basing, a Latin American labour market provides the fighters, and Sudanese civilians provide the casualties. Reader takeaway: this is the documentary evidence that bolts UAE complicity to the RSF's worst conduct, and the OIC silence on it is itself the story. Sudan is OIC; feed offered no Sudanese outlet on this report — note feed-side gap.

stories.label: Residents pack up to leave Dahiyeh before Eid al-Adha as Netanyahu threatens to 'intensify strikes'
stories.summary: Mada Masr's reporter follows named Dahiyeh families packing on Eid al-Adha eve as Netanyahu publicly threatens to intensify strikes on Beirut's southern suburbs — and the Iran ceasefire is being negotiated in Doha at the same hour. Lead with the named family and the calendar: Eid is being spent on the road again, and the ceasefire that was supposed to be regional is not protecting Lebanon. Mechanism worth teaching: 'ceasefire' as Washington defines it covers the US-Iran kinetic front only, and Israel's Lebanon campaign sits outside the deal by design. Reader takeaway: the people of Dahiyeh are the test of what the agreement is actually worth — and this morning they are voting with their suitcases. Egyptian/Lebanese regional voice carried by Mada Masr (EG).

stories.label: Why Xi Jinping is going to Pyongyang
stories.summary: Xi's upcoming Pyongyang visit is the first by a Chinese president since 2019, and Lowy reads it as Beijing tacitly endorsing North Korea's nuclear status while staking a mediator claim ahead of Washington. Lead with the diplomatic sequencing: Xi is visiting before any Trump–Kim re-engagement, which positions China as the broker rather than the spoiler. Mechanism worth teaching: a P5 state can grant de facto recognition to a nuclear program simply by showing up at the right moment — and that move erodes the same nonproliferation regime that is being invoked against Iran in Doha. Reader takeaway: the South Korean nuclear-submarine roadmap and the Xi–Pyongyang trip are two sides of the same erosion; the bright line is dimming from both ends.

stories.label: BP ousts chairman over governance and conduct concerns
stories.summary: BP chairman Albert Manifold was ousted abruptly over governance and conduct concerns just months into the role — a multi-source story carried by GB, US and QA wires. Lead with what the board is admitting: the same shareholder coalition that demanded a renewed fossil-fuel strategy now can't keep its own chair. Mechanism worth teaching: oil-major governance is being pulled in opposite directions by activist climate investors and oil-pivot activists, and Manifold is the casualty of the latter faction running out of patience. Reader takeaway: BP's instability is a leading indicator of how the European oil majors are aging out of the strategic clarity that Aramco and ADNOC still enjoy — and it lands the same week oil is back at $100 over the Iran war.

stories.label: India, US strike critical minerals deal: What's in it, why does it matter?
stories.summary: Jaishankar and Rubio signed a framework on mining, processing and recycling of critical minerals and rare earths — multi-sourced across IN and QA. Lead with what Delhi is buying: a tier-one US partnership in the one supply chain China currently dominates, in exchange for opening Indian deposits and refining capacity to American firms. Mechanism worth teaching: the rare-earth race is being reorganised not as a market but as a bilateral-treaty network — first the US–Australia deal, now US–India, with Armenia signed the same day. Reader takeaway: 'eye on China' is the framing Delhi chose for domestic audiences, but the deeper shift is that minerals policy has become a strand of foreign policy that runs through the State Department, not Commerce.

stories.label: Many EU countries ready to join complaint against EC over Russian gas import ban — Fico
stories.summary: Slovak PM Fico says several EU heads of government have privately signalled they may join Bratislava's legal challenge against the European Commission's Russian-gas import ban. Lead with the politics: the bloc's energy-sanctions architecture is being attacked from inside, by member-state governments arguing in court that the Commission overreached on Article 122. Mechanism worth teaching: when sanctions become litigation rather than consensus, the policy loses durability — buyers can keep contracting around the ban while waiting for it to be annulled. Reader takeaway: the post-2022 EU energy unity is now an open courtroom fight, and the Russian gas re-entry route into central Europe runs through the CJEU, not the pipeline.

stories.label: Analyst on China's spent rocket stages: "Things only continue to get worse"
stories.summary: China launched 93 orbital rockets last year and is on track to surpass that in 2026 — but its expendable upper stages keep falling uncontrolled, with debris regularly raining on populated regions and the orbital-debris budget growing faster than anyone else's. Lead with the cadence (93 in 2025, second only to the US) and what 'things get worse' means in practice: a rising probability per launch that a stage re-entry kills civilians on the ground or compounds the Kessler-syndrome problem for everyone in low Earth orbit. Mechanism worth teaching: space sustainability is a regulatory commons, and China has chosen launch volume over deorbit discipline. Reader takeaway: the same country that polices its airspace tightly is treating the upper atmosphere as a global dumping ground, and there is no functioning international forum that can price the externality.

stories.label: When Quiet Undersea Volcanoes Turn Disruptive
stories.summary: Earth's largest volcanic system is the mid-ocean ridge under the sea — long assumed to erupt only quietly. New seafloor data off Iceland shows shallow undersea eruptions can be explosive, with tsunamigenic and atmospheric consequences. Lead with the inversion of the textbook claim: the world's most-monitored above-water volcanoes are not where the next great surprise will come from. Mechanism worth teaching: pressure–depth thresholds for explosive volatile release are lower than assumed when the eruption is shallow and the crust is hydrothermally altered. Reader takeaway: marine-volcanic hazard modelling — which feeds insurance, undersea cables, and Pacific-rim tsunami warning — is built on a quiescence assumption this paper undermines.

stories.label: 'BusPatrol' Put AI Cameras in Tens of Thousands of School Buses. Now They Want to Give Cops Access
stories.summary: BusPatrol — already running AI cameras on tens of thousands of US school buses — plans to scan every license plate the bus drives past and open the data to law enforcement search. Lead with the scale (tens of thousands of buses, daily routes through residential streets) and the mechanism: a stop-arm-violation product is being quietly reinvented as a mass automated license-plate-reader network with the political cover of 'child safety'. Reader takeaway: the surveillance state's next expansion is not a federal contract — it is a private vendor sitting on a fleet of school buses, and the consent that was given (catch drivers who pass stopped buses) is being rewritten without one. The 'school-bus' framing is what makes this a story: it's the wedge any civil-liberties law would have to confront head-on.

stories.label: Millions of People Are Installing Malware on Their Partners' Phones
stories.summary: Zack Whittaker's stalkerware reporting, distilled: consumer-grade spyware sold openly as 'parental control' is installed on millions of partner phones worldwide, the vendors keep getting breached, and victim notification is essentially absent. Lead with the scale (millions, not a niche) and the mechanism: stalkerware is a regulated category nowhere, breaches its own customer databases routinely, and yet Apple/Google still treat it as a tolerable adjacency to legitimate MDM. Reader takeaway: domestic abuse has a software supply chain, and the largest single privacy harm in many households is being delivered by an app store that the same household paid for. This is the accountability-gap counterpart to the BusPatrol story — surveillance is being privatised at both the public and intimate ends of the stack.

stories.label: Lithuania investigates theft of 600,000 state registry records by foreign actor
stories.summary: Lithuania's Prosecutor General says attackers gained access to more than 600,000 records at the Centre of Registers — the state agency that holds property and legal-entity records — and the working assumption is foreign-actor involvement. Lead with the dataset: a property-and-corporate registry is the OSINT key that lets a hostile service map ownership, ultimate beneficiaries, and sanctions-circumvention shells across the whole economy. Mechanism worth teaching: registry breaches are not data-theft for resale — they are pre-positioning for influence operations, asset-targeting and conditional disclosure. Reader takeaway: this lands the same week Lithuania's airspace was breached by a drone and the EU is rallying around Vilnius — the cyber front of that crisis is being opened in parallel, and 600,000 records is plenty to seed years of leverage.

stories.label: Iran Claims It Shot Down US' MQ-9 Drone Amid Peace Talks
stories.summary: IRGC says its air defence downed a US MQ-9 over the Persian Gulf during the ceasefire window — and the story is carried by Iranian, Turkish, Pakistani and Indian outlets with sentimentDivergence 0.27. Lead with the timing collision: the same day as the strikes-during-Doha-talks pattern, Iran is now signalling that its air defences can still hit US ISR over the Gulf, which is the actual military substance behind the [[us-strikes-iran-missile-sites-doha-talks-ceasefire-test]] arc. Mechanism worth teaching: this is the same Reaper class the USAF is backfilling with ULTRA — Iran is destroying the platform faster than the Pentagon can replace it. Strong OIC regional coverage (IR, TR, PK).

stories.label: Iran's Khamenei Says No Going Back For Middle East Rocked by War
stories.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei tells Muslim states the region 'will no longer be a safe haven' for US bases — and the sentimentDivergence across MEE, Dawn and Bloomberg is 1.08, the widest gap of the day. Lead with what 'no going back' actually claims: the post-war regional order is being declared from Tehran while frozen-asset talks continue in Doha. Mechanism worth teaching: Iran is pivoting from defensive posture to a regional-realignment doctrine that calls on OIC states to disinvest from US basing — pairs with [[trump-abraham-accords-mandatory-iran-ceasefire-precondition]] as the counter-offer to Trump's mandatory-normalisation demand. Strong OIC regional coverage (PK via Dawn).

stories.label: OpenAI's Altman says AI unlikely to lead to 'jobs apocalypse'
stories.summary: Altman dismisses the AI-jobs panic in Sydney days after WiseTech's CEO received violence threats over using AI to replace thousands of workers — and the multi-source spread (AU, GB, IN, SG) shows the same denial landing differently in each economy. Lead with the contradiction: the worker-replacement story is already in police hands in Australia while the OpenAI CEO tells a Commonwealth Bank audience the picture is 'very different than we thought'. Mechanism: the AI-labour narrative is being set by AI-firm executives whose product depends on the prediction being wrong, and the Stanford 22–25 cohort data already shows 16% relative employment decline in AI-exposed jobs. Reader takeaway: this is what 'corporate denial as labour policy' looks like.

stories.label: The Suicide Crisis Stalking Sudanese Refugees
stories.summary: New Lines documents a suicide cluster among Sudanese refugees in Cairo after international funding cuts collapsed UNHCR mental-health and cash-assistance programmes. Lead with the named survivors and the funding number: this is what donor fatigue actually produces — a measurable mortality signal in a population the world stopped counting. Mechanism worth teaching: mental-health programmes are the first line cut in any humanitarian budget shortfall, and the resulting deaths are recorded as 'individual tragedies' rather than policy outcomes. Reader takeaway: the Sudan war's casualty count includes the Cairo refugees who survived the bombs and then died from being abandoned. Sudan and Egypt both OIC; feed offered no Sudanese/Egyptian outlet on this investigation — note feed-side gap.

stories.label: Eli Lilly to buy three small vaccine developers
stories.summary: Eli Lilly is buying three early- and mid-stage vaccine developers in a single announcement — a bet that the post-mRNA, post-RFK-Jr. vaccine market needs new owners with balance sheets that can outlast US regulatory uncertainty. Lead with what the three deals signal: Big Pharma is consolidating vaccine R&D at exactly the moment when public-sector vaccine confidence in the US has been politically destabilised. Mechanism worth teaching: when a government withdraws as a credible vaccine purchaser, the pipeline shifts from public-health priorities (paediatric, low-margin) to investor-priced bets (adult, premium). Reader takeaway: vaccine development is being privatised by acquisition while the FDA is being politicised — and the small developers being bought are the institutional memory the public sector is shedding.

stories.label: StablR freezes USDR and EURR after attacker mints $13.5 million in unbacked tokens
stories.summary: An attacker minted $13.5M in unbacked USDR and EURR tokens at European stablecoin issuer StablR; the euro stablecoin EURR is now trading at $0.548 — half its peg — and the dollar stablecoin USDR is at $0.994. Lead with the price collapse and what it proves: stablecoin 'backing' is an issuer-controlled accounting promise, and a single minting-key compromise can destroy the peg in hours. Mechanism worth teaching: the same technical surface that lets stablecoins issue $322B in dollar proxies (per the [[stablecoins-318-billion-exceed-95-nations-fx-reserves]] arc) also lets a single attacker counterfeit at will — there is no equivalent of central-bank reserves to absorb the loss. Reader takeaway: when an EM saver is told 'just hold synthetic dollars', this is the failure mode no one explains.

stories.label: One Stock Story vs Many Sectors: How SEBI Chief Sees Taiwan's Market Surpassing India
stories.summary: Taiwan's market cap hit $4.95T this week, knocking India to sixth place globally — and India's own regulator (SEBI chair Tuhin Kanta Pandey) is framing the loss as a structural feature ('Taiwan is one stock story, India is diversified'). Lead with the inversion: a regulator publicly arguing that being smaller is healthier is what concession-as-strategy sounds like. Mechanism worth teaching: Taiwan's market is essentially TSMC plus AI suppliers — a single semiconductor concentration risk that the rest of the world is now paying for, while India's diversified market grows more slowly because no single sector compounds at 70% annual revenue. Reader takeaway: global equity rankings are now a proxy for AI-supply-chain exposure, and Taiwan is the index.

stories.label: When the grid can't keep up: how South African laboratories handle power outages
stories.summary: Nature reports from inside SAIAB in Makhanda, where over a million aquatic specimens depend on backup generators surviving each scheduled blackout — and where research workflows have been redesigned around Eskom's load-shedding schedule. Lead with the specimen count and the engineering: a million-jar biodiversity archive is now a battery-management problem. Mechanism worth teaching: African research infrastructure isn't slower because of funding alone — it's slower because every experiment is multiplied by the probability the grid stays up, which propagates into citation counts and grant competitiveness. Reader takeaway: when northern labs talk about 'capacity gaps', the most direct gap is voltage, and the global South's scientific output is being throttled by a power systems failure no peer reviewer accounts for.

stories.label: Researchers upcycle pomegranate peel into high-performance water purifier
stories.summary: A Hong Kong chemistry team turned discarded pomegranate peel into a nanoscale carbon material that strips 4-nitrophenol — a persistent industrial pollutant — from water at high efficiency. Lead with the feedstock economics: pomegranate peel is a free, abundant, distributed waste stream across the Mediterranean, Iran, India and South Asia, and the synthesis route here doesn't need rare reagents. Mechanism worth teaching: fruit-waste-derived activated carbons are one of the few water-treatment innovations where the inputs are most abundant in the regions with the worst industrial water contamination. Reader takeaway: this is what 'frugal chemistry' looks like — pollution remediation that scales by going to where the waste is, not by importing equipment.

stories.label: Disease, drought, and conflict: How Yemenis are adapting to a compounding crisis
stories.summary: Global Voices ground report from Yemen: cholera, dengue and respiratory illness are rising in parallel as drought, conflict damage and collapsed sanitation compound — and the public-health response is being run by local volunteer networks rather than the WHO machinery. Lead with the named diseases and the named coping mechanisms: community-led water-chlorination teams, peer-to-peer dengue surveillance, mosque-distributed ORS. Mechanism worth teaching: 'compounding crisis' isn't a slogan — it's the epidemiological pattern where each shock raises the baseline mortality of the next, and the only response left when institutions fail is mutual aid. Reader takeaway: Yemenis are not waiting for the response — they are the response, and the [[yemen-sanaa-antipsychotic-qt-prolongation-cardiac-risk-polypharmacy]] paper shows the cost of running a health system from the bottom up. Yemen is OIC; this is a regional-voice surrogate (Global Voices is global but the reporters and quoted voices are Yemeni).

stories.label: The agentic divide: Why 'good enough' AI isn't enough to survive the new economy
stories.summary: Rest of World documents how AI-agent quality is bifurcating into two tiers: well-resourced firms get high-trust autonomous agents that scale infinitely, while small operators in the global South are stuck with 'low-trust' agents that require constant human supervision and produce more friction than they save. Lead with the mechanism: agent quality is gated by inference compute and proprietary tool integration, both of which are cheap-at-scale and prohibitive at the small-business level. Reader takeaway: 'AI democratisation' rhetoric is now empirically false — the agent gap is producing a productivity divide between global-North enterprises and their global-South suppliers that compounds with every contract. This is the structural follow-on to [[asean-ai-agent-swarm-disinformation-southeast-asia-exposure]] on the labour side.

stories.label: Kremlin appoints cyber executive with alleged GRU ties to Security Council role
stories.summary: Andrei Kozlov — formerly running Rostec's cyber-security centre and reportedly tied to GRU — has been made an aide to Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu. Lead with the institutional move: the Russian state is consolidating offensive cyber, defence-industrial cyber, and national-security strategy under one person in Shoigu's office. Mechanism worth teaching: the Western analytic distinction between 'civilian cybersecurity' and 'military cyber operations' does not exist in the Russian structure, and the Rostec-to-Security-Council pipeline is how it's enforced. Reader takeaway: when the next major Russian cyber operation surfaces, the doctrine behind it is being written in the office this appointment just staffed — and Shoigu's portfolio now formally includes the offensive side.

stories.label: Ceasefire extended: Digital rights don't pause
stories.summary: SMEX (Beirut-based digital-rights org) argues the Iran-war ceasefire window is not a digital-rights pause — surveillance, internet throttling, account takedowns and platform compliance with state requests across Lebanon, Iran, Syria, Yemen and Gaza continued through the ceasefire. Lead with what 'ceasefire' actually means online: kinetic operations stop but the digital occupation does not, and the Mideast platform-compliance landscape has tightened during the war window, not loosened. Mechanism worth teaching: digital-rights regimes ratchet during wars and never fully reset — every wartime moderation rule that gets normalised becomes the peacetime baseline. Reader takeaway: this is what an OIC regional civil-society voice sounds like on the day Khamenei declares 'no going back' — pairs with [[khamenei-no-going-back-us-bases-middle-east-realignment]] as the civil-liberties counterweight to state-realignment rhetoric. SMEX (Lebanon) IS the regional voice here.

stories.label: Von der Leyen to head to Lithuania for drone crisis talks
stories.summary: EU Commission president travels to Vilnius after a stray drone triggered Lithuanian air alerts, with Baltic presidents convening on shared defense financing. Lead with the mechanism: a single drone incursion is now sufficient to mobilize an EU-wide procurement conversation — the Baltic states have effectively turned every airspace violation into an industrial-policy event. Note that NATO has yet to articulate a doctrine for sub-attack incursions, which is the real gap this trip is meant to paper over.

stories.label: Safe Enough? East Palestine, Emergency Spending, and Who Gets Protected
stories.summary: Three years after the Ohio derailment, residents are still tracking unexplained illnesses while Congress fast-tracks war supplementals worth orders of magnitude more than the EPA's East Palestine relief. Lead with the asymmetry of 'emergency': money moves in days for foreign conflicts and in years for domestic chemical poisoning, and the same federal agencies invoked safety reassurances in both contexts. The accountability hook is that the residents being told the air was safe are the same constituency on whose behalf the war budget is justified.

stories.label: Starbucks Korea's Tank Day Promotion on a Massacre Anniversary Causes a Political Firestorm
stories.summary: A corporate marketing 'Tank Day' promotion launched on May 18 — the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju massacre, when South Korean army tanks killed pro-democracy protesters — has reopened the country's unresolved fight over authoritarian memory. Lead with the date collision: 46 years on, the symbol of the regime's violence is still close enough to the surface that a coffee chain stumbled into it. The structural angle is how South Korea's democratic transition deferred reckoning, leaving public memory to be policed by consumer outrage rather than institutions.

stories.label: At $318 billion, the stablecoin market value exceeds the FX reserves of 95 nations
stories.summary: Stablecoin supply has hit $322 billion — larger than the foreign-exchange reserves of 95 sovereign nations combined, with the bulk backed by US Treasuries. Lead with the inversion: a privately issued dollar-proxy now exceeds the official dollar holdings of most of the world's central banks, creating a parallel monetary plumbing that emerging-market regulators can neither inventory nor restrict. The structural angle is capital-flight acceleration — when a Nigerian or Argentine saver can hold synthetic dollars in a wallet, the local currency loses a buyer of last resort. Name the policy gap: most of those 95 countries have no enforcement reach against Tether or Circle issuers.

stories.label: More Iran war? There goes the neighborhood, and world economy.
stories.summary: IEA data shows a cumulative one-billion-barrel shortfall in Gulf oil deliveries since the war began, absorbed by a 250-million-barrel drawdown in global inventories that IEA chief Birol calls 'unsustainable.' Lead with the distribution of pain: Somalia's refugee-camp grain transport has tripled in cost, Kenya saw four protest deaths over fuel, Indian migrant workers can no longer afford black-market LPG. The structural angle is that the same war that pushed US energy export revenues up $50 billion has cost US consumers $40 billion at the pump — but Global South households absorb the rest. Frame around WFP's projection that 45 million additional people face acute hunger if the war drags on.

stories.label: Sulfonamide resistance as a global one health challenge
stories.summary: E. coli isolates now show 44–57% resistance to sulfamethoxazole worldwide, with 93% of resistant strains carrying sul1 or sul2 — the same two genes circulating across humans, livestock, and soil. Lead with the percentage and what it means: a frontline antibiotic introduced in the 1930s is now compromised in roughly half of clinical E. coli cases globally. The mechanism worth teaching is integron-mediated horizontal gene transfer, which lets a resistance cassette jump between unrelated bacteria in environments saturated with sub-therapeutic antibiotic residues — agricultural runoff, sewage, factory effluent. This is what 'one health' actually means: AMR is an environmental contamination story, not just a hospital story.

stories.label: Borno records 2,700 suspected cholera cases, 27 deaths in May
stories.summary: 2,715 suspected cases and 27 deaths across five LGAs in 24 days — a case fatality rate near 1%, consistent with a system that can rehydrate patients but can't reach them in time. Lead with the geography: Borno is the heart of the ISWAP/Boko Haram insurgency, so the same security collapse that lets the conflict run also blocks water-and-sanitation infrastructure and routine surveillance. The accountability angle is that Nigeria has the WHO-prequalified oral cholera vaccine available but hasn't pre-positioned it in the northeast despite annual outbreaks. Name the structural failure: cholera in 2026 is a logistics indicator, not a microbial one.

stories.label: Satellites track SO₂ emissions following March 2026 refinery fires in Tehran, Iran
stories.summary: A research team used Sentinel-5P, TROPOMI and TanSat data to reconstruct the SO₂ plume from the March 7 explosions at Tehran's oil storage and refining sites — quantifying a pollution event the Iranian government did not publish ground measurements for. Lead with the method: free, open satellite data now lets researchers audit wartime industrial damage to civilian air quality in real time, independent of state cooperation. The structural angle is that this same technique works for any siege, strike, or refinery fire — making remote sensing the de facto accountability instrument when domestic monitoring has been silenced. Note the public-health consequence: Tehran civilians breathed measurable SO₂ that no agency told them about.

stories.label: S. Korea to Deploy Locally Built Nuclear Submarine by Late-2030s
stories.summary: South Korea unveiled a roadmap for an indigenously built nuclear-propulsion submarine, first launch mid-2030s, first deployment late-2030s — quietly demanding revisions to the US–ROK 123 Agreement to allow enrichment above 20%. Lead with the fuel: a nuclear sub requires highly enriched uranium that Seoul is currently barred from possessing, and 'locally built' is shorthand for renegotiating a 50-year-old nonproliferation cap. The structural angle is that two US allies (Korea, Australia under AUKUS) are now on parallel paths to nuclear-naval propulsion, eroding the bright line that justified denying the same capability to Iran and Brazil. North Korea's submarine threat is the framing, but the precedent reaches well beyond the peninsula.

stories.label: China's "Bohai Sea Monster" Reappears With Apparent Weapons Hardpoints
stories.summary: New imagery of China's wing-in-ground-effect (WIG) heavy transport — the so-called Bohai Sea Monster — shows fixtures consistent with external weapons stations, recasting it from a logistics platform into a potential strike system. Lead with the physics: WIG craft fly at wave-top altitude, below radar coverage, with payloads on the order of a cargo aircraft and the speed of a ship-killing missile cruise. The structural angle is that the only previous serious WIG program was the Soviet Caspian Sea ekranoplan, abandoned for engineering reasons in the 1980s — China appears to have solved those problems with modern materials and is the first state to militarize the concept since. The Taiwan Strait is the obvious operating area.

stories.label: USAF's New Turbocharged ULTRA Surveillance Drones Are Heading To The Middle East
stories.summary: The US Air Force is deploying ULTRA — a turbocharged glider-derived long-endurance surveillance drone — to CENTCOM specifically to backfill MQ-9 Reaper attrition from the Iran war. Lead with the cause: Iranian air defenses shot down enough Reapers that the Pentagon is now substituting a slower, cheaper, less-detectable airframe — a tacit admission that the Reaper era over contested airspace is closing. The structural angle is the same lesson visible in Ukraine's fiber-optic drones: when sophisticated systems prove vulnerable, militaries don't go up the tech stack, they sideways into harder-to-jam, harder-to-shoot alternatives. ULTRA's persistence-over-payload tradeoff is the new shape of ISR in contested zones.
